expansion: The lecture's episcleritis slide describes exactly this presentation: "Relatively common, benign and self-limited cause of red eye... Presented with: Red eye, Mild pain and/or discomfort, Mild localised ocular tenderness, No discharge (if present: minimal & watery)" (L13,14, slide 30), which matches a painful, tender, localised, non-discharging redness. The lecture also notes episcleritis is usually unilateral, consistent with a single localized area of redness rather than a diffuse allergic process (L13,14, slide 30). Bulbar spring catarrh (vernal keratoconjunctivitis affecting the bulbar conjunctiva) is fundamentally an ITCHY allergic condition with papillary or limbal changes, not a tender, non-itchy localized redness, so it does not match this stem's key negative feature of being non-itchy (not taken from the course material, but excluded by its defining itch). Vascular pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth encroaching on the cornea from the conjunctiva; it may become inflamed and red but presents as a visible growth rather than a localized, tender patch of redness without a mass lesion, so it does not fit this description either (not taken from the course material). Phlyctenular conjunctivitis produces a small nodular hypersensitivity lesion at the limbus that is typically associated with photophobia, tearing and foreign-body sensation from an accompanying corneal component, rather than the mild, purely localized tenderness the lecture assigns to episcleritis, and the lecture does not describe it as tender and non-itchy in this way (not taken from the course material). Episcleritis, with its lecture-defined combination of localized redness, mild tenderness, absence of itching, and absence of discharge, is the best match for the stem.
objective: Recognise episcleritis from painful, tender, non-itchy localized conjunctival redness
